title: Enzymes: Life's Catalysts
hook: The chemical reactions that keep you alive would crawl too slowly to matter — enzymes speed them up millions of times without being used up themselves.
key_points: Enzymes are mostly proteins that act as biological catalysts.
They speed up reactions by lowering the energy needed to start them.
Each enzyme has a specific shape that fits only certain molecules.
Enzymes are not consumed, so one molecule works again and again.
content_html: Most of the reactions inside you wouldn't happen fast enough to keep you alive — at body temperature, they'd take years instead of seconds. Enzymes solve that problem. These molecules, almost all of them proteins, are catalysts: they dramatically speed up chemical reactions without being changed or used up themselves, so a single enzyme can do its job over and over.
extra_html: An enzyme works by lowering a reaction's activation energy, the initial hump of energy needed to get it going. It does this by grabbing its target molecules at a pocket called the active site, whose shape fits only certain partners — often compared to a lock and key. That specificity means your cells run thousands of different enzymes, each tuned to one task, from digesting food to copying DNA. As Encyclopaedia Britannica notes, life's entire web of chemistry depends on these proteins quietly accelerating reactions that would otherwise grind to a halt.

related.title: Metabolism
related.hook: Every breath, heartbeat, and thought runs on metabolism — the vast web of chemical reactions that builds your body up and breaks your fuel down.

related.title: ATP: The Cell's Energy Currency
related.hook: Cells don't store usable energy as sugar or fat alone — they spend it through ATP, a tiny rechargeable molecule that powers almost everything they do.

related.title: The Digestive System
related.hook: From the first bite to the final absorption, your digestive tract is a one-way assembly line that turns food into fuel your cells can use.

flashcards.back_html: A biological catalyst — usually a protein — that speeds up a chemical reaction in a living thing without being used up in the process.

flashcards.prompt: How do enzymes speed up reactions?

choices.text: By lowering the energy needed to start the reaction
By adding heat to the reaction
By becoming part of the final product

flashcards.explanation_html: Enzymes reduce the activation energy — the push a reaction needs to begin — so reactions that would otherwise be far too slow can happen quickly at body temperature.

flashcards.prompt: Why is each enzyme specific to certain molecules?

choices.text: Its shape fits only particular molecules, like a lock and key
It can speed up any reaction equally
It is consumed after each reaction, so it can only act once

flashcards.explanation_html: An enzyme's precisely folded shape creates an active site that fits only its target molecules — the classic lock-and-key idea — which is why each enzyme handles a specific job.
